title: Medical Office Replacement Sourcing
name: Medical Office Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Medical Office Replacement Sourcing in Fort Worth, TX
metaDescription: Sourcing and documenting medical office replacement candidates near Fort Worth's hospital campuses, with lease and tenant-credit review before identification.

sections.html: Medical office buildings trade on lease documentation as much as on location, and a Fort Worth candidate that looks sound on a broker flyer can carry lease terms that do not hold up once a qualified intermediary and a lender both need to rely on them. Sourcing for this asset class means pulling the lease file before the property goes on an identification list, not after.

sections.heading: Where Medical Office Inventory Concentrates in Fort Worth
sections.html:
The heaviest concentration of physician-occupied and hospital-affiliated office space sits near the Near Southside and Cultural District medical corridor, where campus-adjacent buildings house specialty practices, imaging groups, and ambulatory surgery tenants tied to the hospital systems anchoring that district. Smaller stand-alone medical buildings are scattered through suburban corridors closer to where physicians' patient bases have grown, and those properties carry a different tenant profile than campus-adjacent space.

We source from both segments because an exchange investor's risk tolerance for a single-tenant physician group differs from the risk profile of a multi-tenant building carrying a mix of specialty leases.

Ownership structure adds another layer to sourcing in this asset class, since some campus-adjacent buildings near the medical corridor are held as medical office condominiums with individual unit ownership rather than as a single whole-building asset. A condominium unit carries its own association documents, reserve funding requirements, and voting rights that a whole-building acquisition never has to address, and we confirm which structure applies before a Fort Worth candidate is added to a comparison list.

sections.heading: Tenant Credit and Lease Structure Review
sections.html:
A physician group's personal guaranty is only as strong as the practice's billing and payer mix, and a solo or small-group tenant carries materially different credit risk than a practice affiliated with a larger health system. We request the tenant's lease abstract, any corporate or practice-level guaranty, and confirmation of whether rent escalations are fixed or tied to an index, since medical office leases in this market are inconsistent on that point.

Triple-net medical leases also vary in how they define reimbursable operating expenses, and a building with ambiguous CAM language can leave the buyer absorbing costs the seller's own numbers never reflected.

Tenant improvement allowance history deserves separate attention, since a landlord who fronted a large TI package for a physician group's clinical buildout typically amortizes that cost into the rent over the lease term. A buyer who does not confirm the remaining unamortized balance can inherit a lease priced to recover a cost that was never fully collected, understating the real economics of the space once the current term expires.

sections.heading: Documentation to Request Before Identification
sections.html:
Before a medical office building is added to a 45-day identification list, we assemble a defined document set rather than relying on the listing broker's summary.

  • full lease abstract for every suite, including renewal options and termination rights
  • tenant improvement allowance history and any unamortized landlord contribution
  • certificate of occupancy and any medical-use zoning confirmation
  • estoppel certificate request drafted for signature at or before closing
  • base building systems inspection covering HVAC zoning specific to clinical space

sections.heading: Lease Renewal Exposure and Rollover Risk
sections.html: Medical tenants relocate less often than typical office tenants once clinical buildout costs are sunk, but a lease approaching its renewal option inside the first two years of ownership still needs to be underwritten as a rollover risk rather than assumed stable. We flag any lease where the renewal option rent is undefined or subject to a fair-market reset, since that gap can materially change the property's income once the option period arrives.

sections.heading: Coordinating the 45-Day Window Around Medical Real Estate Timing
sections.html: Medical office sellers and their lenders sometimes move slower than a standard commercial closing, particularly when a hospital system holds a right of first refusal or a consent requirement tied to an affiliated tenant. We confirm those consent rights early in the identification window so a Fort Worth exchange does not stall waiting on a signature the seller could have obtained weeks earlier.

faqs.q: What makes medical office lease review different from standard commercial office review?
faqs.a: Medical leases often carry personal or practice-level guarantys tied to a physician group's billing and payer mix rather than a corporate credit rating, and clinical buildout costs make tenant relocation less likely but the guaranty strength still needs independent verification.

faqs.q: Why does a hospital system's right of first refusal matter for exchange timing?
faqs.a: A consent or right-of-first-refusal clause tied to an affiliated tenant can delay closing beyond a standard commercial timeline, and confirming that requirement early in the identification window prevents it from threatening the 45-day or 180-day deadlines.

faqs.q: How is CAM ambiguity handled in a triple-net medical office lease?
faqs.a: We review how operating expenses are defined in each lease before identification, since inconsistent CAM language across suites can leave a new owner absorbing costs the seller's trailing numbers never reflected.

faqs.q: What happens if a medical tenant's renewal option has no defined rent?
faqs.a: An option subject to a fair-market reset rather than a fixed rate is underwritten as a rollover risk, not assumed stable, because the income at renewal could differ meaningfully from the current lease rate.

faqs.q: Is a single-tenant medical building riskier than a multi-tenant building for a replacement property?
faqs.a: It depends on the tenant's credit and lease guaranty strength rather than the tenant count alone, though a multi-tenant building spreads lease-rollover risk across several practices instead of concentrating it in one.

faqs.q: Why does it matter whether a medical office unit is condominium-owned or part of a whole building?
faqs.a: A condominium unit carries its own association documents, reserve funding obligations, and voting rights that a whole-building acquisition does not have to address, and confirming that structure before comparison affects both diligence scope and ongoing management responsibilities.
